newsitem.title: INDIA: Thanks, we have enough, India banks tell depositors.
newsitem.headline: Thanks, we have enough, India banks tell depositors.

text.p: Flush with funds and faced with a shortage of profitable areas to deploy them, several Indian banks are turning away large depositors, bankers and analysts said on Wednesday.
The strategy is aimed at avoiding a situation where interest payments on deposits would exceed earnings, analysts said.
Bankers said they were not turning away all depositors but only those from whom no other business could be expected.
"Basically the issue here is one of benefits to the bank," said P.H. Ravikumar, senior vice-president at ICICI Banking Corporation.
"Retail deposits are regarded as core deposits and are always acceptable to banks," Ravikumar said. "But large short-term deposits from companies are different."
These were more in the nature of "hot" deposits which would move out of the bank at short notice, Ravikumar said.
"Therefore we exercise some discretion in such cases. If the prospective depositor is already a customer with us and has say, a loan or other facility with us, we accept the funds."
"Liquidity with the banking system is just too easy at the moment," said Amit Rajpal, banking analyst at Prime Broking. "Banks are struggling to find profitable uses for their funds."

Bank deposits have grown by 9.6 percent or 417.26 billion rupees from April 1, 1996 to January 17, 1997 against a growth of 208.03 billion or 5.4 percent in the same period last year according to latest data released by the Reserve Bank of India.
Advances have grown by 4.5 percent or 115.11 billion rupees compared to 294.89 billion (13.9 percent) in the same period.
Rajpal said poor growth in bank credit disbursals coupled with low yields on short-term securities was forcing a number of banks to reject deposits.
Banks offer interest between 7.5 percent per annum and 10 percent for deposits from 30 days to less than one year, depending on their maturity.
Yields on government securities range from 6.5 percent to 9.8 percent for maturities between 30 days and around one year.
Loans offer much better returns.
The prime lending rate, charged to the highest-rated borrowers, ranges from 14.5 percent charged by leading Indian state-run banks to 18.5 percent by foreign banks.
"It does not make commercial sense to accept deposits in this scenario unless credit disbursals pick up," said the chairman of a south India-based state-run bank, who asked not to be named.
"I have asked my officers to make sure that we have proper (profitable) uses for funds before accepting them."
Some banks however take a different view.
"There is no question of our not accepting deposits," said Pandurang Kakodkar, chairman State Bank of India, India's largest commercial bank.
"The problem with money is that you will not get it when you need it. You therefore do not take chances," he said.
